articles.title: UNICEF Viet Nam El Niño Early Warning Situation Report No. 1 (June –19 August 2026)
articles.description: Please refer to the attached file. Situation Highlights • On 24 July 2026, the Government confirmed that “El Niño 2026–2027 has taken shape,” increasing the risk of severe drought, water shortages and saltwater intrusion in Viet Nam. • NOAA Global Outlook3 (13 August 2026): El Niño is further strengthening, with a >90% chance of a "very strong" event continuing through winter 2026-27, and during the October-December 2026 season, there is a 69% chance of a historic event that would exceed the strength of previous El Niño events dating back to 1950 (+2.5°C or more). • Government planning scenarios: Under the high-risk scenario, El Niño reaches moderate-to-strong intensity and rainfall, and river flows could be 10–20 per cent below average. Under the very-high-risk scenario, El Niño becomes very strong and rainfall and river flows could be 20–40 per cent below average. These are probability-based scenarios, not certainties. • Priority regions and impact window: The South-Central Coast, Central Highlands and Mekong Delta are assessed as very-high-risk regions. The most critical impacts are expected from late 2026 to May 2027, including prolonged drought, extreme heat, water shortages, reduced river flows, depleted reservoirs and saltwater intrusion. • Children and essential services face rising risks from reduced safe water, food and livelihood insecurity, higher food prices and disruption to water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) services, health, nutrition, education, child protection and social protection services. • Children most at risk: Children under five; pregnant and breastfeeding women; children with disabilities; children from poor and ethnic minority households; migrant children; and children in remote, coastal, drought-prone and water-insecure communities. • No widespread El Niño-related humanitarian needs have been confirmed to date, making the current lead time critical for anticipatory action, risk communication, frontline readiness and continuity of essential services. • Maintain multi-hazard readiness: El Niño does not remove the risk of typhoons, extreme rainfall, flash floods, landslides and urban flooding. Preparedness must therefore remain multi-hazard. • Past El Niño events show the cost of delayed action and the value of preparedness: in 2015–2016, 2 million people lacked sufficient domestic water and 1.1 million were food insecure; earlier forecasting and community action helped reduce losses in 2023–2024. Preparedness financing is needed ahead of the anticipated February–May 2027 peak-impact period.

articles.title: ‘Super El Niño’ Could Make 2026 the Hottest Year Ever
articles.description: A strengthening El Niño pushed ocean temperatures in a key part of the Pacific to record highs in September and is on track to make 2026 the hottest year on record, the director of the EU’s climate monitoring services said Monday. Global forecasters have predicted for months that this year’s El Niño could be the most intense one yet, but its September highs have come weeks before its December peak. The previous record for daily sea surface temperatures in the central-eastern Pacific in September was set during the 2015 El Niño. As oceans warm due to climate change, it has become harder to compare recent El Niño events with past ones. The Copernicus Climate Change Service said it has adopted a new index to account for warming oceans. Copernicus director Carlo Buontempo said this year’s El Niño is “very exceptional,” but it is too early to tell whether it will be the strongest on record yet. El Niño is a naturally recurring climate pattern that happens about every two to seven years and temporarily raises sea surface temperatures in the tropical Pacific. Read it at Yahoo! Read more at The Daily Beast.

articles.title: After the flood: supporting recovery, reconstruction and resilience in Nepal
articles.description: Emma Gogerty, Sarah Opitz-Stapleton, Kanchan Mani Dixit The devastating flood and debris flow along the Nepal–China border on 26 August caused an estimated $2.7 billion in loss and damage. Total recovery and reconstruction needs are likely to exceed $4.8 billion according to the Government’s Rapid Damage and Needs Assessment. As of 3 October 2026, 1,455 bodies have been recovered and over 5,200 remain missing; these numbers could climb as information comes in from hard-to-reach communities. Furthermore, the disaster caused cascading damage and disruptions to local agricultural, fishing, and forestry livelihoods and markets. Emergency relief is, of course, essential. But relief is only the first stage of a longer process of recovery, reconstruction and – ultimately – resilience. This stage is typically the most under-funded. It is also where sustainable development organisations tend to make their most lasting contribution – if they stay long enough to get there. The theme of this year’s International Day for Disaster Risk Reduction (marked annually on 13 October) is ‘Resilience Starts at Home’. Typically after a disaster, affected people are the first responders – they ‘self-recover’ out of necessity, relying on their ‘own and local resources, often with little or no external assistance’. Following a disaster on the scale of the August flood and debris flow, in communities where poverty already exceeds the national rate, there is only so much self-recovery and disaster-resilient reconstruction that can be done. The evolving landscape of disaster risk reduction in Nepal The Gorkha earthquake in 2015 holds a number of lessons for policy and practice on how to support people to recover and rebuild. The government played a critical role in supporting recovery through the provision of cash grants, financial assistance and training to support owner-driven reconstruction. However, tranches were conditional and housing recovery was slow, due to ‘householders’ lack of access to relevant, timely information and affordable materials for construction, together with mounting debts and complications relating to land tenure’. Since the earthquake, risk governance and the landscape of humanitarian action in Nepal have changed considerably. There has been a transition away from responding to crises towards managing risk, with enhanced state responsibility to manage disasters. In 2017, the Disaster Risk Reduction and Management (DRRM) Act came into force, and a National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA) was established in 2019. The Strategic Action Plan for Gender Equality, Disability and Social Inclusion in Disaster Risk Reduction and Management, endorsed by the NDRRMA Executive Committee in 2024, recognises the need for an intersectional approach to reducing vulnerability and building the capacity of different groups to manage shocks. The harder problem is translating policies into action at the local level. A national disaster strategy means very little to a family living beside a dangerous river if that family has no knowledge of the evacuation route in the event of a flood. A national climate policy offers no protection to a farmer whose land has disappeared under water. A disaster management framework, however well written, cannot save a child if the early warning it promises never reaches that child’s village. This is precisely where sustainable development organisations can be most useful: not in writing new policy, but in helping to translate existing policy into resilience at the community level. From early warning to response and recovery in the aftermath of the flood, the NDRRMA has been working with ministries and in coordination with provincial and district-level governments, NGOs and community groups. The government has released $1.06 million in cash relief for three districts, restored electricity and cell phone connectivity and deployed additional health workers. Grants and in-kind relief from international humanitarian organisations, philanthropies, governments and others are supporting the Nepali government’s immediate response and early recovery efforts. However, since the Gorkha earthquake, Nepal has not faced a disaster of this scale, where policies, governance structures and financing have been put to such a test. The coming months will bring into stark relief what aspects of the pivot from disaster response to preparedness and risk mitigation are working well, and what challenges remain. It also presents a chance for the government to consider how to strengthen and integrate climate change risk management into reconstruction and recovery, including supporting local efforts and capacity- building. Nepal will not be able to achieve these things without international support. Climate justice and compensation Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal has referred to the disaster as a ‘direct consequence of global climate change’. As such, ‘We are shifting our diplomatic framework from “aid” to “justice and compensation”. This is not a matter of charity; it is a matter of legal and moral liability. The major industrial emitters … have a historical responsibility to compensate vulnerable nations like Nepal’. Nepal has requested $20 million in climate-related flood compensation from the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage (FRLD). However, to date the FRLD (created at COP27 in 2022 and adopted at COP28 in 2023) has not paid out any funds, despite over 119 requests. With looming multi-country impacts expected from the 2026–2027 El Niño, the FRLD is likely to get many more requests, despite having received only about 30% of the funds pledged by wealthy countries. The lack of fund disbursement in relation to existing requests, including Nepal’s, raises real questions around climate justice, and whether wealthy countries will honour their climate and disaster financing commitments. Nepalis can only ‘self-recover’ so much. And the government, from the local to federal level, has finite resources for recovery, reconstruction and climate adaptation even as climate-related hazards continue to increase in frequency and severity. While Nepal has invested significantly in glacial-lake outburst floods (GLOF) monitoring, the August flood has highlighted the need to broaden this effort through earth observation, wider hazard monitoring, risk communication and transboundary data-sharing to identify evolving risks and support timely action. Greater efforts are required to support households and communities in integrating climate adaptation into flood recovery and reconstruction efforts, without locking in climate change risks. ‘Official reconstruction policies, regulations and conditions affect the speed of recovery trajectories and progress towards safer building’, often with unintended consequences. This leads to broader questions around state responsibility – including embedding climate change resilience within disaster risk management, reconstruction and development – and how the international community can support this process. This will also require the government to prioritise climate adaptation in its planning and overall oversight of development. National blueprints will not work; instead, it is important to recognise that people have different recovery trajectories that will change over time, based on ‘changing needs and priorities, livelihood pressures, psycho-social reactions to the disaster’ and the level of technical skills, resources and information available. Recognising different recovery trajectories, and supporting these through flexible and adaptable programming, is key.

articles.title: World: UN calls for greater investment in housing resilience as homes account for 43% of reported disaster losses
articles.description: GENEVA, 13 October 2026 – Housing accounts for 43 per cent of direct economic disaster losses reported by countries through the Sendai Framework Monitor, highlighting the urgent need for greater investment in safer homes and household preparedness, the United Nations Office for Disaster Risk Reduction (UNDRR) said today. Marking the International Day for Disaster Risk Reduction, under the theme Resilience Starts at Home, UNDRR is calling on governments, the private sector and communities to make housing resilience a priority – from where homes are built and the standards they meet to how families prepare for and recover from disasters. “Safety begins where we live, and preparedness at the household level – understanding the risks, having a plan, and acting swiftly – can mean the difference between life and loss,” said United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres. Data reported by countries through the Sendai Framework Monitor also show that around half of the people reported as affected by disasters experienced damage to or destruction of their homes. Beyond the economic costs, the loss of a home can displace families, disrupt livelihoods and undermine physical and psychological wellbeing. Global risk modelling by the Coalition for Disaster Resilient Infrastructure (CDRI) further illustrates the scale of housing risk. Under current climate conditions, its Global Infrastructure Risk Model and Resilience Index estimates average annual losses of approximately US$228 billion for residential buildings from cyclones, floods, tsunamis and earthquakes – representing 53 per cent of estimated annual losses across the world's building stock from these two hazards. Eleven years after the adoption of the Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction, progress in reducing disaster mortality has not been matched by comparable progress in reducing the number of people affected by disasters or the economic cost of disasters. "Until housing becomes safer and more resilient, we will not be able to significantly reduce the number of people affected by disasters and their cost," said Kamal Kishore, Special Representative of the United Nations Secretary-General for Disaster Risk Reduction and Head of UNDRR. With millions of people still lacking adequate and affordable housing, efforts to close the global housing gap represent an important opportunity to prevent the creation of new disaster risk. UNDRR is calling for resilience to be integrated into housing policies, urban planning and investment decisions, including through the selection of risk-informed locations, adoption and enforcement of resilient building standards, and investment in retrofitting existing homes and infrastructure. Depending on the hazards they face, homes must be able to withstand earthquakes, floods, cyclone winds or extreme heat, including under future climate projections. When disasters do occur, housing recovery should be prioritised because of its importance to wider social and economic recovery. Homes damaged or destroyed should be rebuilt to higher standards, to avoid the recreation of past vulnerabilities while ensuring that affected households are engaged in the recovery process. Resilience at home also depends on whether households understand the risks they face and are prepared to act when disasters threaten. New findings from the Lloyd's Register Foundation World Risk Poll 2026 highlight the importance of household preparedness. Among people who had experienced a disaster and received an advance warning, just 27 per cent of those who had neither a household disaster plan nor confidence in their ability to protect themselves or their families were able to act on the warning, compared with 83 per cent of those who had both. The findings also reveal inequalities in the ability to act across income groups, underscoring the need for governments to ensure that households have access to risk information, early warnings and the resources needed to take protective action. The International Day for Disaster Risk Reduction calls for a global movement bringing together governments, communities, businesses and households to make homes safer and ensure that families are equipped to protect themselves. Reducing disaster impacts will require both: homes that are built to last, and households that are empowered to act. Themes Disaster losses Shelter and housing

articles.title: World: Bridging the early warning to action gap requires building resilience at home
articles.description: Bridging the early warning to action gap requires building resilience at home When disasters are imminent, timely warnings can be the difference between life and death. However, warnings are only effective when they are received, understood, and acted on. That is why the theme of the 2026 International Day for Disaster Risk Reduction (IDDRR), “Resilience Starts at Home,” aims to raise awareness of the need to strengthen the physical resilience of homes while ensuring that households have the resources, information, plans and confidence they need to protect themselves. New findings from the Lloyd's Register Foundation World Risk Poll 2026 report, ‘Alert to Agency’, reveal an important gap between receiving an early warning and taking action. Across the countries and territories surveyed, four in five people who had experienced a disaster in the previous five years reported receiving at least one warning beforehand. Yet only 64% of those who received a warning said they were able to take action because of it. For every 100 people impacted Pictogram of 100 people impacted by a disaster: about 51 were warned and able to act, 29 were warned but not able to act, and 20 were not warned. Warned and able to act: about 51 Warned but not able to act: 29 How people are reached also matters Among those receiving a warning through one channel, 37% were able to act, rising to 51% among those reached through two channels and 64% among those reached through three. But communication is only part of the equation. The findings suggest that what happens next depends in part on the resilience of the household receiving the warning. Preparedness and a sense of personal agency make a substantial difference. Among people who had been impacted by a disaster and received an advance warning, 83% of those with both a household disaster plan and a sense that they could protect themselves or their family were able to take action. That compares with just 27% of people who had neither a preparedness plan nor a sense of personal agency. Having a plan alone was associated with 50% taking action, while having a sense of agency alone was associated with 60%. Share of warned adults able to take action, by household plan and confidence Household plan No sense of agency Sense of agency This 56-percentage-point gap shows that resilience at home is not simply about receiving information. It also depends on whether people are prepared and feel able to act. The World Risk Poll data, available on the Early Warnings for All Dashboard, measures resilience at four levels – individual, household, community and societal – and finds that while global resilience remains unchanged from 2023, Africa saw the largest regional improvements, driven largely by gains in household resilience. Many of the largest increases in household resilience globally have been recorded in some of Africa’s most populous countries. Between 2021 and 2025, household resilience increased by 13 points in Algeria, nine in Nigeria, eight in Kenya, seven in Egypt and six in Uganda. The reasons behind these increases are not uniform. Household resilience in the World Risk Poll combines people’s financial assets and ability to meet basic needs, the existence of household plans for a disaster, and access to communications in the form of the internet and mobile phones. Improvements can therefore come through different pathways. One of these is connectivity. Internet access has increased across all four African regions since 2019, potentially strengthening households’ access to early warnings, information, essential services and social support. Improved connectivity does not automatically create resilience, but it expands access to early warnings and access to risk information. This information enables households to better understand the hazards they can expect, their levels of exposure based on location, and the potential vulnerability of their cities or homes. This full understanding of risk can then influence their decisions on where to live, how to build or reinforce their homes, and what actions to take in response to early warnings. At the same time, the report makes clear that preparedness is not simply a matter of individual responsibility. The ability to act in response to warnings is influenced by a country's income level. Under half of respondents in low-income (48%) and lower-middle-income (47%) countries said they were able to take action as a result of a warning. This compares to around three-quarters of respondents (71%-75%) in upper-middle and high-income countries. Governments therefore have a critical role in creating the conditions that enable people to prepare and act. This means investing in reliable and inclusive early warning systems, ensuring that risk information is accessible and actionable, supporting household preparedness and planning, and addressing the financial and practical barriers that can prevent people from taking protective action. People prepare and act Reliable and inclusive early warning systems Risk information that is accessible and actionable Household preparedness and planning Addressing financial and practical barriers Governments: creating the conditions As countries work towards the goal of Early Warnings for All, the measure of success cannot be simply whether a warning was sent or received. It must be whether people were able to use it to protect themselves and their families. That is also the message at the heart of the 2026 International Day for Disaster Risk Reduction: resilience starts at home, but it depends on the systems, services and support that make household action possible.

articles.title: What's burning in Indonesia that's responsible for haze reaching the Philippines?
articles.description: Jakarta, Indonesia—For weeks on end, parts of Indonesian Borneo have resembled an Armageddon landscape with masked residents immersed in a putrid, red-brown haze as wildfires devour peatlands near homes and farms. Burning slowly, mostly under the surface and sometimes for months on end, peatland fires are responsible for much of the dry season haze that this year has tainted air as far afield as Malaysia, Singapore and the Philippines. articles.title: Republic of the Marshall Islands Launches Strategic Roadmap for Health and Coastal Infrastructure Resilience
articles.description: Please refer to the attached file. The Government of the Republic of the Marshall Islands (RMI), in partnership with UNOPS, has officially launched the "Roadmap for Health and Coastal Infrastructure Resilience of the Marshall Islands." The newly released Roadmap provides an evidence-based framework designed to ensure that essential health services and coastal assets remain functional and accessible during extreme weather events and rising sea levels. Developed through detailed gap assessments and climate readiness evaluations, the initiative translates local vulnerability data into actionable long-term infrastructure planning for the Marshallese government. The framework is aligned with national policies and priorities, including the National Strategic Plan, National Adaptation Plan, National Infrastructure Investment Plan and the Sustainable Development Goals. It also sets out prioritised actions, financing pathways and institutional responsibilities to support coordinated resilience investments. To deliver tangible outcomes for local communities, implementation will focus on six core strategic priorities. The framework addresses long-term operations and maintenance management, climate-proofing outer island health clinics, and establishing an integrated geospatial asset and hazard information system. Additionally, the plan prioritizes scaling up nature-based coastal protection, strengthening emergency shelter readiness, and delivering phased resilience upgrades along the Majuro Airport to Laura Road corridor. Gender equality, disability, and social inclusion are integrated across the strategic framework. Through the application of universal design principles and inclusive infrastructure planning, future investments in health facilities, coastal protection, emergency shelters, and other essential infrastructure can support safe and equitable access for women, men, persons with disabilities, older people and other community members. Marking the formal completion of the project's assessment phase, the launch event brought together Secretary-level leadership from the Ministry of Health and Human Services (MoHHS) and the Ministry of Public Works, Infrastructure, and Utilities (MPWIU), alongside representatives from the Coalition for Disaster Resilient Infrastructure (CDRI) and UNOPS management. “For the Ministry, this Roadmap comes at a very useful time. In the Marshall Islands, almost every infrastructure decision is affected by where and how we live. We build on narrow strips of land. We work in a highly corrosive marine environment. We deal with flooding, erosion, saltwater, high waves, and limited space. At the same time, we have to serve communities spread across many islands and atolls. So for us, resilience is not an abstract idea. It is a very, very practical question,” said Walter Myazoe, Secretary of the Ministry of Public Works, Infrastructure and Utilities (MPWIU). “The Roadmap can only show us the direction, but we all have to take this journey together. We have to build resilience into the way we design, budget, construct, maintain and deliver health services. I hope this Roadmap is seen not as the finish line of a planning process, but as the beginning of a stronger partnership between health and public works” said Francyne Wase-Jacklick, Secretary of the Ministry of Health and Human Services (MoHHS). “The launch of this Roadmap marks an important step towards strengthening the resilience of health and coastal infrastructure in the Marshall Islands. For Small Island Developing States, where communities and critical infrastructure face significant climate and disaster risks, resilience needs to be integrated into infrastructure planning and investment from the outset. CDRI is proud to fund this project through the Infrastructure Resilience Accelerator Fund, helping translate vulnerability assessments and local priorities into a practical roadmap for resilient infrastructure investment. We hope the Roadmap will help the Marshall Islands protect essential services, strengthen communities and build long-term resilience to a changing climate,” said Ramesh Subramaniam, Global Director - Programmes & Strategy, CDRI. “This Roadmap transitions our shared efforts from technical gap assessments to long-term, actionable infrastructure planning. By establishing clear national priorities from climate-proofing outer island health clinics to strengthening asset maintenance systems, we are equipping the Marshall Islands with a strategic blueprint to guide resilient investments and ensure essential services remain uninterrupted during climate shocks.” said Nicholas George, Director of UNOPS South East Asia and the Pacific Multi Country Office. UNOPS extends its gratitude to the Governments of India, Australia, and the United Kingdom, and to the European Union, for their financial support through the Coalition for Disaster Resilient Infrastructure's Infrastructure Resilience Accelerator Fund (CDRI IRAF).
